subject: religious-studies
title: Acts, Ends, and Double Effect
welcome_lead: Enter the casuist's chamber, where Natural Law refines itself through the doctrine of double effect.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on real vs apparent goods, interior/exterior acts, and the doctrine of double effect.
final_note: Natural Law's subtleties show how ancient theory still navigates modern dilemmas.

concepts.def: An action genuinely aligned with the natural law and human flourishing.
An action that appears desirable but, on rational analysis, is contrary to natural law.
The intention or motive of an action, central to its moral evaluation.
The outward action itself, evaluated together with intention.
A principle permitting an action with both good and bad effects, provided the bad effect is foreseen but unintended.
A 20th-century Catholic revision (e.g. Bernard Hoose) allowing 'proportionate reasons' to override traditional moral absolutes.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Aquinas argues that all rational action aims at some good. When reason is functioning well, it perceives real goods aligned with natural inclination and flourishing.

When reason is clouded by passion or ignorance, we may pursue apparent goods (e.g. revenge as 'justice') that do not in fact serve human flourishing.

The moral quality of an act depends on both the exterior deed and the interior intention. An act good in itself (e.g. giving alms) becomes morally defective if done for vainglory.

Conversely, no good intention can render intrinsically evil acts (e.g. blasphemy, adultery) permissible.

The DDE, rooted in Aquinas' discussion of self-defence (ST II-II, q. 64, a. 7), permits an act with two effects (one good, one bad) if four conditions hold: the act itself is not intrinsically evil; the good effect is intended; the bad effect is not the means to the good; and proportionate grounds exist.

It is applied in modern bioethics to cases such as palliative sedation and the removal of a cancerous uterus in pregnancy.

mcqs.q: The doctrine of double effect is rooted in which question of the Summa Theologica?
options: II-II, q. 64, a. 7 on self-defence
I, q. 2 on God's existence
I-II, q. 90 on law
I-II, q. 1 on happiness

mcqs.q: Proportionalism is associated with which 20th-century Catholic theologian?
options: Bernard Hoose
Karl Rahner
John Henry Newman
Hans Kung

mcqs.q: What does natural law theory base morality on?
options: Human nature and reason — there are objective purposes (telos) built into humans which reason can discover, generating universal moral precepts.
Natural law means whatever happens in nature is morally right.
Natural law is the same thing as the laws of physics.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.

mcqs.q: What does utilitarianism say is right action?
options: Natural law is the same thing as the laws of physics.
Whatever makes you personally happy is the right thing to do.
The action that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number — judged by consequences, not intentions or rules.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.
